chunk_findings.detail: `anchors()` only counts repeats of the *base* slug and never checks that the suffixed result is itself free, so it can emit the same anchor twice, contradicting its own docstring ("a repeat numbered ... as GitHub does"). Concretely, given headings `## Foo`, `## Foo-1`, `## Foo` (in that order), `slug()` yields `foo`, `foo-1`, `foo`; `anchors()` returns `["foo", "foo-1", "foo-1"]` because the third heading's `seen["foo"]` is 1 and it never notices `foo-1` is taken. `render()` therefore emits two TOC entries that both link to `#foo-1`, while GitHub's slugger resolves the third heading to `#foo-2` (it retries suffix 2 after `foo-1` collides). The result is exactly the class of bug this change exists to prevent: a link in the generated table of contents that dangles on GitHub. The same collision occurs for any heading whose title already ends in a number matching a duplicate's suffix (e.g. `## Step 1`, `## Step 1`, `## Step 1-1`).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/views/readme_toc.py:anchors

chunk_findings.detail: `dead_anchors()` builds its `known` set from `headings()`, which only matches `#{2,3}`, so level-1 (`#`) headings — and any other level — are treated as if they had no anchor, even though GitHub generates anchors for them. Given a README containing `# ddflow` and a prose link such as `[ddflow](#ddflow)`, this function returns `["ddflow"]` and reports a dead anchor even though `#ddflow` is a valid target on GitHub, which fails `tests/test_readme_toc.py` on an otherwise correct README. The docstring's claim ("In-page links that match no heading") is therefore too broad for what the function actually checks.

chunk_findings.detail:
`render()` computes duplicate-suffix numbers over only the headings it lists (`##`/`###`, minus `TOC_TITLE`), but GitHub assigns ids to *all* headings of every level in document order, so the numbering diverges as soon as a level-1 or level-4..6 heading shares a slug with a listed heading. Given

```
## Foo

#### Foo

### Foo
```

`headings(readme)` yields `[(2,"Foo"), (3,"Foo")]` and `anchors` returns `["foo","foo-1"]`, so the TOC becomes `- [Foo](#foo)` / `  - [Foo](#foo-1)`. On GitHub the ids are `#foo` (## Foo), `#foo-1` (#### Foo), `#foo-2` (### Foo), so the second TOC entry points at the `####` heading, not the `###` section. The same happens with a level-1 duplicate (`# Foo` then `## Foo`: the `##` entry gets `#foo`, i.e. the page title). Note this is *not* answered by the `used`-set fix for the earlier "`Foo`, `Foo-1`, `Foo`" finding: that fix only deduplicates inside the sub-list; the list itself is incomplete, so the emitted suffix is still wrong. `dead_anchors()` cannot catch it either, because it builds `known` from `headings(readme, _ANY_HEADING)` (all levels), so `#foo-1` is considered a live target even though it is the wrong section.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/views/readme_toc.py:80 (`render`, via `anchors`)

chunk_findings.detail:
The fence state machine only inspects the leading run (`_FENCE` captures `` `{3,}|~{3,} `` and ignores the remainder), so a fence-looking line carrying an info string is accepted as the closing fence, although CommonMark only closes a block on a line followed solely by spaces. Given

```
## Real

```text
```python
## Fake
```
```

the line ` ```python ` matches `_FENCE`, `run[0] == fence[0]` and equal length, so `fence` is cleared and the following `## Fake` is collected as a real heading: `render()` emits `- [Fake](#fake)`, but on GitHub `## Fake` is code inside the ```text block, there is no `#fake` id, and the generated link is dead. `dead_anchors()` does not flag it (the link lives in the stripped TOC region, and its own fence-stripping regex does require the close to be pure fence characters, so the two functions disagree), and the equality test passes because `render` is self-consistent.

chunk_findings.detail: Headings are matched with `^(#{1,6}) +...` and `^(#{2,3}) +...`, i.e. only at column 0, while the fence regex two lines above explicitly allows a ` {0,3}` prefix. CommonMark/GitHub accept ATX headings indented by up to three spaces and give them anchors, so `  ## Install` is an `h2` with anchor `#install` on GitHub but is invisible to `headings()`. Input: a README containing the (indented) heading `  ## Install` plus the perfectly valid prose link `[install](#install)`. `headings()` returns no entry for the heading, so `render()` silently drops it from the generated table of contents, and `dead_anchors()` computes `known` without `install` and reports the valid link as dead — the new test fails on a README that GitHub renders correctly. The same ` {0,3}` allowance used for fences should be used for the heading patterns.

chunk_findings.detail: `known = set(anchors([t for _lv, t in headings(readme, _ANY_HEADING)] + [TOC_TITLE]))` appends `"Table of contents"` to the heading titles even though the region's heading is *outside* the region markers and is therefore already returned by `headings()` (that is why `render` has to exclude `t == TOC_TITLE` from the listing). With the normal README (exactly one such heading) `anchors()` therefore emits both `table-of-contents` and `table-of-contents-1`; input: a README with `## Table of contents` and the link `[x](#table-of-contents-1)` — an anchor that no heading in the document produces — is accepted, i.e. the check this change exists to add ("a test that fails when an anchor in the README points nowhere") silently passes a dead link. If the heading is ever renamed/absent, the same line additionally injects a phantom `table-of-contents` anchor.

data.title: ddflow/views/readme_toc.py:102 (`dead_anchors`)

chunk_findings.detail: `headings()` decides whether a line closes a fence with `not line.strip(run[0] + " ")` (line 47), which accepts a closing fence followed by spaces — legal CommonMark (a closing fence may be followed only by spaces/tabs), and what `headings()` must accept so headings after such a block are still found. The regex used by `dead_anchors` to blank out code blocks, `r"^ {0,3}(`{3,}|~{3,}).*?^ {0,3}\1[`~]*$"`, instead requires the closing line to end in fence characters (`[`~]*$`), so a closing fence with trailing whitespace never matches. Input: a README whose code block is closed by a line `` ``` `` with a trailing space, containing a line like `[example](#example-anchor)` where `#example-anchor` names no heading. `headings()` correctly treats the block as closed (so `render` is right), but in `dead_anchors` the `re.sub` has no matching close, so no stripping happens, the literal text inside the code block is scanned by `re.findall(r"\]\(#([^)\s]+)\)", prose)`, and `example-anchor` is returned as dead even though it is code, not a link — `tests/test_readme_toc.py` then fails on a correct README. (With a second, well-formed block present the same regex pairs the first opening with the *later* block's close and deletes intervening prose, hiding genuinely dead anchors instead.) The two implementations of the same rule should be unified or the regex extended to allow trailing spaces (and reject interior spaces, which `line.strip(run[0] + " ")` also wrongly accepts).
